headline: Kirai is the stem form of the verb 嫌う (kirau, “to detest, dislike, hate”).

sources.quote: /kiraɸi/ → /kirawi/ → /kirai/
From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 嫌(きら)う (kirau, “to detest, dislike, hate”).

headline: Aoi was Old Japanese awosi, from awo-, from Proto-Japonic *awo.

sources.quote: Modern form of Old Japanese adjective あをし (awosi); from Old Japanese awo-, from Proto-Japonic *awo.
⟨awosi⟩ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → ⟨awoki₁⟩ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /aoi/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 萬 (MC mjonH). Compare modern Cantonese 萬 /万 (maan⁶), Hokkien 萬 /万 (bān).

sources.quote: From し (shi, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb する (suru, “to do”)) + 合(あ)い (ai, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 合(あ)う (au, “to do to each other; to do together”)).

headline: Naku is 音 (na, “(emotional) sound, voice”) plus く (-ku, verb suffix), cognate with 鳴く (naku).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, derived from 音 (na, “(emotional) sound, voice”, bound form) + く (-ku, verb suffix). Cognate with 鳴(な)く (naku).

meaning: four days; fourth day of the month
headline: Yokka is considered a shift from 四日 (yoka), a compound of 四 (yo, “four”) plus 日 (-ka, counter for days).

sources.quote: Considered to be a shift from 四日(よか) (yoka) below. Ultimately a compound of 四(よ) (yo, “four”) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days).

headline: Hako was pako, and originally referred to a kind of wicker basket or box introduced from continental Asia.

sources.quote: /pako/ → /fako/ → /hako/
From Old Japanese pako. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *pako.

This term originally referred to a kind of wicker basket or box introduced from continental Asia, and the word is thought to be a borrowing from, or cognate with, a predecessor form of modern Korean 바구니 (baguni, “basket”). Compare Middle Korean 바고니〮 (pàkwòní).

headline: Otto was wofito, a compound of 男 (wo, “male, man”) plus 人 (fito, “person”), first attested in roughly 1220.

sources.quote: Shift from older unattested 男(を)人(ひと) (wofito), synchronically analyzable as a compound of 男(を) (wo → o, “male, man”) + 人(ひと) (fito → hito, “person”).
Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *wopitə, with many Ryukyuan cognates.
First attested in roughly 1220.

headline: Okurimono is 贈る (okuru) plus 物 (-mono).

sources.quote: 贈(おく)る (okuru) + 物(もの) (-mono)

headline: Kokoro is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kəkərə.

sources.quote: ⟨ko₂ko₂ro₂⟩ → */kəkərə/ → /kokoro/
From Old Japanese 心 (ko₂ko₂ro₂), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kəkərə. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Compare Okinawan 心 (kukuru).

headline: Abiru comes from the classical upper bigrade verb 浴ぶ, possibly from 浴む (amu).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb (バ行上二段活用) 浴ぶ, possibly from Old Japanese 浴む (amu), in the 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.
Cognate with Okinawan 浴みゆん (amiyun).

headline: Haizara is 灰 (hai, “ash”) plus 皿 (sara, “plate”), and sara changes to zara by rendaku.

sources.quote: 灰 (hai, “ash”) + 皿 (sara, “plate”). The sara changes to zara as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Karui was seldom used outside of proper nouns in Old Japanese, spelled 軽 in the Man'yōshū.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, in turn from Proto-Japonic *karu. In Old Japanese, seldom used outside of proper nouns, where in the Kojiki it is spelled as 加流 and in the Man'yōshū it is spelled as 軽, suggesting that this word was already used in Old Japanese with the meaning "light, lightweight". This might be weakly strengthened by a kana annotation of 軽 as karu(ku) in the Nihon Shoki.

It is generally believed that karu(si) was the older form; this is also supported by Ryukyuan cognates (see Proto-Ryukyuan *karu). In the Heian period and Kamakura period, the variant かろし (karoshi) → かろい (karoi) has started to be in use, while 軽し (karushi) → 軽い (karui) has still seldom usage.
Later, both karosi and karusi began to be used in parallel. Then, in Early Modern Japanese, karui slowly began to replace karoi.

headline: Iu was ipu: the p became an f sound, then w, and a w before u never surfaced.

sources.quote: /ipu/ → /iɸu/ → /*iwu/ → /iu/ → /juː/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ipu.

Medial /p/ regularly changed from [p] → [ɸ] → [w]. Japanese never distinguished between /wu/ and /u/, so that automatically becomes [u]. The /w/ only surfaces in the negative form of iwanai, where the phoneme sequence /wa/ exists. Surface forms /iwimasu/ and /iwemasu/ automatically became /iimasu/ and /iemasu/ since Japanese no longer distinguishes /wi, we/ from /i, e/.

headline: Yoko is from Proto-Japonic *yəkə, with cognates in Kunigami, Miyako, Okinawan and Yaeyama.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yəkə. Cognate with Kunigami 横 (ゆく゚ー, yukū), Miyako 横 (ゆく, yuku), Northern Amami Ōshima 横 (ゆく゚, yuxu), Okinawan 横 (ゆく, yuku), Yaeyama 横 (ゆく, yuku), Yonaguni 横 (どぅぐ, dugu).

sources.quote: Compound of 図(と)書(しょ) (tosho, “books”) + 館(かん) (-kan, “building”).

sources.quote: Doublet of 務(つと)める (tsutomeru).

sources.quote: From 奥様(おくさま) (okusama); equivalent to 奥(おく) (oku) + さん (san).

headline: Manga was manɡwa, coined in Japan from Middle Chinese-derived 漫 (man, “as one pleases”) plus 画 (ga, “picture”).

sources.quote: /manɡwa/ → /manɡa/
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese‐derived elements, as a compound of 漫(まん) (man, “as one pleases”) + 画(が) (ga, “picture”).
The sense of a drawing first appears in 1798 in the foreword to Santō Kyōden's picture book 四(し)時(じの)交(ゆき)加(かい) (Shiji no Yukikai), already using the modern shinjitai spelling of 漫画.
The archaic sense of “Eurasian spoonbill” is attested even earlier in the 1778 medical text 薬(やく)品(ひん)手(て)引(びき)草(ぐさ) (Yakuhin Tebikigusa).

In the late nineteenth century, the term was repurposed as a translation for the English word caricature. This shift was led by artists such as Imaizumi Ippyō and Kitazawa Rakuten to elevate satirical drawings (formerly known as ポンチ絵(え) (ponchi-e)) into a professional art form. It later expanded to encompass sequential “comics” as that medium gained popularity in the early twentieth century.

headline: Suteru is from Old Japanese 捨つ (sutsu), a lower bigrade verb.

sources.quote: From 下二段 (shimo nidan) verb 捨つ (sutsu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 捨つ entry.
